items.prompt: A depth-first recursive traversal visits each of n real tree nodes once. Let h be the number of real nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. Which statement gives tight asymptotic bounds in these parameters?
constraints: The structure is a tree with no shared or cyclic nodes.
Each real node is visited exactly once.
Per-node local work is O(1).

options.text: Time is Θ(n), and recursion-stack space is Θ(h).
Time is Θ(h), and recursion-stack space is Θ(n).
Time is Θ(n), and recursion-stack space is Θ(n) for every tree shape.
Time and stack space are exponential because each node may make two recursive calls.

feedback.reason: Total work counts all visited nodes, while stack space counts only the longest active ancestor path.

blocks.text: Depth-first recursion suspends a parent while one descendant path is explored. At any instant, the active frames correspond to one root-to-current path, so the extra call stack is proportional to tree height h. Across the complete run, however, each of the n nodes is entered and processed, giving O(n) time when per-node work is constant. A skewed tree has h = n; a balanced tree has h = O(log n). This distinction between total call count and maximum simultaneous call depth is the central accounting boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_h_stack_n: Height bounds one active path, not the total nodes visited. Every node contributes work even when the tree is shallow.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_n_stack_n_always: Linear stack is tight only for a skewed tree. In a balanced tree h = Θ(log n), and only one root-to-leaf path is simultaneously active.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_exponential: The calls go to disjoint child subtrees and each real node is visited once. Branching does not imply repeated exponential states.

items.prompt: Order the runtime events for sumTo(2), where sumTo(0) returns 0 and sumTo(n) returns n + sumTo(n - 1).
constraints: Evaluation of n + sumTo(n - 1) waits for the recursive call to return.
The runtime uses ordinary last-in, first-out call-stack semantics.

elements.text: The frame for n = 2 is created and suspends while requesting sumTo(1).
The frame for n = 1 is created and suspends while requesting sumTo(0).
The n = 1 frame resumes, computes 1 + 0, and returns 1.
The n = 2 frame resumes, computes 2 + 1, and returns 3.

feedback.reason: Recursive calls push suspended frames until the base returns, then results flow back in reverse call order.

items: Create the n = 2 frame; it cannot add yet, so it requests sumTo(1) and remains suspended.
Create the n = 1 frame; it requests sumTo(0) and also remains suspended.
The n = 0 frame returns the base value 0. At this deepest point, three frames are alive.
Last-in, first-out unwinding resumes n = 1 first; it returns 1 + 0 = 1.

blocks.text: Each suspended frame retains its own parameter and return continuation. This isolation explains why recursive locals do not overwrite one another and why extra stack space follows maximum simultaneous depth rather than total calls over the whole run.

items.prompt:
factorialAcc(n, acc) returns acc when n == 0; otherwise it returns factorialAcc(n - 1, acc * n).
The target runtime does not guarantee tail-call optimization. What is the correct stack conclusion?
constraints: n is a non-negative integer.
The runtime does not guarantee tail-call optimization.
Arithmetic cost and overflow are outside this item's scope.

options.text: The call is in tail position, but maximum stack usage is O(n) without a guaranteed optimization.
Stack usage is O(1) because a tail-position call automatically reuses the frame.
Stack usage is O(2^n) because factorial grows exponentially in value.
No stack frame is needed because acc contains the partial result.

feedback.reason: Tail recursion changes the continuation shape, but stack complexity remains runtime-dependent unless tail-call elimination is guaranteed.

blocks.text: The recursive call is the final operation, so the current frame has no pending arithmetic after the child returns. A compiler or runtime may exploit that fact by replacing the call with a jump and reusing one frame. The content contract, however, states that such optimization is not guaranteed. Under ordinary call semantics, n, acc, and return control are represented by one frame per call, giving depth O(n). The transfer rule is to separate source-level tail position from an implementation-level tail-call guarantee.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_stack_by_syntax: Tail position makes frame reuse possible, not mandatory. Without a language/runtime guarantee, ordinary calls can retain one frame per decrement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exponential_stack: Numeric result magnitude does not determine call depth. There is one recursive child and n decrements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_stack: The accumulator removes post-return arithmetic, but the function call itself still needs runtime control state unless optimized into iteration.

items.prompt:
A function processes a range of n elements. For n > 1 it splits the range into two disjoint halves,
recursively processes both halves, and does O(1) local combining work. Each one-element range is terminal.
Select the tight time and extra recursion-stack complexities.
constraints: The halves are disjoint and together cover the parent range.
Local work and local frame data are O(1).
The split is balanced to within one element.
The implementation evaluates recursively using depth-first call-stack semantics.

feedback.reason: The disjoint recursion tree contains O(n) total nodes, while balanced depth keeps only O(log n) frames active at once.

blocks.text: The time recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1). The n one-element leaves and fewer than n internal combine nodes give total O(n) work. Stack space is not the sum of frames across the whole tree: depth-first evaluation completes one branch before its sibling, so only one root-to-leaf path plus constant sibling bookkeeping is active. Balanced halving produces O(log n) depth. The result changes if each frame allocates an n-sized copy or if the split is highly unbalanced; those costs are excluded by the stated constraints.

items.prompt:
maxFrom(i) returns the maximum of the non-empty suffix a[i:] in an array of length n > 0.
It stops at i == n - 1 and otherwise calls maxFrom(i + 1). What is the maximum number of simultaneously
active maxFrom frames from maxFrom(0)?
constraints: The input array is non-empty.
The function is never called with i == n.
The runtime does not perform tail-call optimization because comparison remains after the child returns.

options.text: n frames, including the singleton base frame.
n + 1 frames because every recursive function must add an empty-suffix base frame.
One frame because each call replaces the previous call.
2^n frames because recursive maximum is exponential.

feedback.reason: The legal suffix states are i = 0 through n - 1, and all n corresponding frames are live at the deepest point.

blocks.text: The base case is the one-element suffix, not an invented empty suffix. Starting at i = 0, recursion creates frames for every valid index through n - 1. Just before the singleton returns, n frames are active. The parent frames are suspended because each still needs to compare its local element with the child's return. This directly counters the empty-only base heuristic and shows its resource consequence: stack accounting follows actual reachable states, not a universal template that adds one more empty call.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_plus_one_empty: The declared domain is non-empty suffixes, and i == n - 1 already supplies the atomic answer. An empty frame is neither called nor required.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_frame: The parent still needs its a[i] value and continuation to compare with the child maximum, so ordinary calls remain suspended until unwinding.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_power_n: There is one child per non-terminal frame, creating a chain rather than a branching call tree.

items.prompt:
sumFrom(i) computes rest = sumFrom(i + 1) and then returns a[i] + rest.
While processing a three-element suffix, which statement about rest is correct?
constraints: rest is a function-local variable.
No global or captured mutable variable named rest is used.
The runtime uses ordinary call frames.

options.text: Each active frame owns a separate rest slot that receives its own child's return value.
All calls share one rest variable because the source code uses the same name.
rest exists only in the base frame.
Every rest value is identical because every call executes the same statement.

feedback.reason: A recursive invocation creates a new frame, so identically named parameters and locals are isolated per call.

blocks.text: When sumFrom(0) calls sumFrom(1), the first frame remains suspended with its own i and future rest slot. The child creates a second frame, and so on. During unwinding, each child sum is stored in the rest slot of its immediate parent, producing different values for different suffixes. This frame isolation is why ordinary recursive code can retain ancestor context without explicit arrays. Shared behavior occurs only for deliberately global, captured mutable, or reference-shared objects—not merely because local names repeat.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_shared_rest: A local variable belongs to a call frame. Reusing its source-level name does not make the storage or value global.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rest_exists_only_base: The base may return directly, while every non-terminal parent needs its own rest value after the child completes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rest_values_identical: The same statement runs on different suffix states, whose sums can differ. Uniform code does not imply uniform local values.

items.prompt:
countdown(n) has a correct base n == 0 and calls countdown(n - 1). For a very large n on a runtime with a
bounded call stack and no tail-call optimization, which conclusion is correct?
constraints: n is finite and non-negative.
The runtime stack is bounded.
Tail-call optimization is not guaranteed.

options.text: The recurrence terminates mathematically, but execution may raise stack overflow before reaching the base.
The base case guarantees successful execution for every finite n.
A stack overflow proves the recursive transition does not make progress.
The runtime must convert any one-call recursion into a loop.

feedback.reason: Strict descent proves a finite call sequence, while bounded stack capacity imposes an independent maximum practical depth.

blocks.text: The measure n decreases to zero, so the abstract computation has finite depth n + 1. Under ordinary call semantics, however, all ancestor frames remain live until the base returns. A runtime with a smaller stack limit can fail partway through that finite sequence. This is not logical nontermination; it is resource exhaustion. The transfer rule is to evaluate both obligations: prove progress for correctness, then compare maximum depth and per-frame cost with the execution environment or replace deep recursion with iteration.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.base_guarantees_execution: A termination proof does not guarantee sufficient runtime resources. O(n) simultaneous frames can exceed a fixed stack limit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.overflow_means_nonterminating: The transition can strictly decrease n and still exhaust finite memory before the terminal state is reached.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.runtime_converts_to_loop: Such optimization is language- and implementation-dependent and cannot be assumed under the stated constraints.

items.prompt:
length(node) returns 0 for None and otherwise returns 1 + length(node.next).
The input is an acyclic list of n real nodes, and each frame does O(1) local work.
Select the tight time and extra recursion-stack complexities.
constraints: The list is finite and acyclic.
Each node is reached exactly once.
Per-frame local data is O(1).
The runtime does not eliminate these non-tail frames.

feedback.reason: One call is created per node and all ancestor frames remain active until the None result unwinds.

blocks.text: The call graph is a single path through n real nodes plus one terminal None call, so total call count and time are O(n). Because each parent must add one after its child returns, ordinary evaluation retains the entire chain of frames at maximum depth, giving O(n) extra stack space. No branch duplicates work, so exponential time is unsupported. The distinction also shows why replacing recursion with an iterative pointer walk can preserve O(n) time while reducing auxiliary control space to O(1).

items.prompt: A recursion advances one array index per call and performs O(1) local work. What auxiliary space does the call stack use?

options.text: O(n), because up to n frames remain active before unwinding.
O(1), because each frame has only constant local variables.
O(n²), because every frame stores the full array.
O(0), because the compiler removes all recursive frames.

feedback.reason: The stack measures simultaneous active frames, not just the local variables in one frame.

blocks.text: Although each frame is constant size, a depth-n chain keeps n frames alive before the base case returns. An iterative rewrite may reduce this auxiliary stack to O(1).

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_stack: Constant local frame size does not imply constant maximum depth.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadratic_stack: Frames hold references and scalars, not a full array copy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_stack: Ordinary recursion requires active call frames unless transformed by a guaranteed optimization.

items.prompt: In a balanced divide-and-conquer recursion on n items, which quantity primarily determines stack depth?

options.text: The longest root-to-leaf path, typically O(log n) when each split halves the input.
The total number of leaves, which is always the stack depth.
The total number of operations across every branch, regardless of overlap in time.
The numeric values, even when split sizes are fixed.

feedback.reason: Only one active branch is followed at a time, so depth is the height of the recursion tree rather than its total node count.

blocks.text: A balanced halving recurrence has O(log n) active frames even if the total work across all subproblems is O(n log n) or larger.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.leaf_count: Leaves describe total branching work, not simultaneous ancestors on one path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.total_work: Completed sibling calls are no longer active while another branch is explored.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_values: Fixed split sizes determine depth here, not the data values.

items.prompt: What determines the auxiliary stack space of a recursive routine that makes one child call at a time?
constraints: Each call remains active until its child returns.
The maximum active depth is h.

options.text: O(h) auxiliary stack space, where h is the maximum recursion depth, even if total work is larger.
options.explanation: Only simultaneously active frames occupy the call stack.

options.text: O(n) stack space whenever total work is O(n), regardless of depth.
options.explanation: Work and active depth are separate measures.

options.text: O(1) stack space because calls return automatically.
Space equals the number of recursive branches ever created.
options.explanation: Completed branches no longer occupy the stack unless stored.

feedback.reason: Recursive space is peak active frames, not total calls over the entire execution.

blocks.text: A linear chain has O(n) depth; a balanced divide-and-conquer routine can have O(log n) depth while doing O(n) total work. State both when they differ.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.work_n: Work and active depth are separate measures.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.branch_count: Completed branches no longer occupy the stack unless stored.

items.prompt: Why can a recursive routine have exponential time but only linear stack space?
constraints: Each call may make multiple recursive calls.
Calls are evaluated depth-first.

options.text: The recursion tree can contain exponentially many total calls, while depth-first evaluation keeps only one root-to-leaf path active at a time.
options.explanation: Time counts all calls; stack counts peak simultaneous frames.

options.text: Every recursive call remains active until all branches finish, so stack must equal total call count.
options.explanation: Completed sibling branches return before the next is explored.

options.text: Exponential time implies memoization is already present and limits stack.
options.explanation: The distinction holds even without memoization.

options.text: Branching does not affect time because only the deepest path is evaluated.
options.explanation: All branches contribute to total work.

feedback.reason: Depth-first recursion separates total recursion-tree size from active call-stack depth.

blocks.text: A naive Fibonacci-style routine repeats subproblems exponentially, but its call stack is bounded by the maximum argument depth. If calls are scheduled concurrently, the space model would differ and must be stated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exponential_stack: Completed sibling branches return before the next is explored.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memoized: The distinction holds even without memoization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_time: All branches contribute to total work.

items.prompt: What does tail-recursion optimization change in the space analysis when the language guarantees it?
constraints: The recursive call is the final operation of the function.
The runtime reuses the current frame for tail calls.

options.text: The optimized tail-recursive path can use O(1) stack space, although the logical recursion depth may still be O(n).
options.explanation: Frame reuse changes implementation space, not the mathematical state progression.

options.text: Tail optimization makes a linear number of calls logarithmic time.
options.explanation: It changes stack storage, not call count.

options.text: Tail recursion removes all state because parameters are not needed after the call.
options.explanation: Parameters are carried into the next iteration.

options.text: Every language and runtime automatically performs tail-call elimination.
options.explanation: The guarantee is language and implementation dependent.

feedback.reason: Tail-call elimination is a runtime contract that can collapse active frames into iterative state.

blocks.text: Without the guarantee, the same source recursion may use O(n) stack. Complexity reports should distinguish logical depth from guaranteed implementation space.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_log: It changes stack storage, not call count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_state: Parameters are carried into the next iteration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_optimized: The guarantee is language and implementation dependent.

items.prompt: How should memoization change the space accounting of a recursive overlapping-subproblem solution?
constraints: There are O(s) distinct memo states.
The recursion can have depth h.

options.text: Report O(s+h) auxiliary space in the straightforward implementation: memo storage plus peak active recursion frames.
options.explanation: Memoization and call stack are separate consumers.

options.text: Report O(s) because memoization eliminates every active recursive frame.
options.explanation: Frames remain active during the top-down computation.

options.text: Report O(h) because memo entries are output rather than auxiliary state.
options.explanation: Memo entries are stored working state unless explicitly reused as output.

options.text: Memoization affects only time, never space.

feedback.reason: Top-down dynamic programming commonly uses both a memo table and a call stack.

blocks.text: The exact bound depends on state representation and recursion scheduling, but omitting either memo storage or active frames understates auxiliary space.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memo_only: Frames remain active during the top-down computation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stack_only: Memo entries are stored working state unless explicitly reused as output.
